article: Cyberpunk's signature palette — hot neon pink and cyan against wet, light-polluted black — is really a photograph of a very particular kind of city street, repeated for forty years. The genre's literary roots run to the early 1980s, when writers including William Gibson (whose 1984 novel Neuromancer gave the genre its clearest text) imagined futures where technology had made life faster and more connected but also meaner and more unequal, with megacorporations replacing governments. Its visual identity, though, was set less by any book than by Ridley Scott's 1982 film Blade Runner, which rendered that future as permanently rain-slicked night: towering neon signage, mostly in advertising-signage pink and cyan, reflected endlessly off wet pavement and dense urban haze. That look drew heavily — and, especially in retrospect, controversially — on real Hong Kong and Tokyo street photography, borrowing the density and signage of real Asian cities as backdrop and atmosphere for Western-authored stories, a pattern later cyberpunk media (including 2020's Cyberpunk 2077) has had to reckon with. Color-wise, the genre's black is never a flat, dry black the way goth's is; it's always wet, always catching a reflection, which is part of why cyberpunk's palette reads as more alive and more oppressive at once than a simple neon-on-black description suggests.
